titre: John Snow's Proof Was Not the Broad Street Pump
accroche: On September 8, 1854, the pump handle is removed while the epidemic is already receding; Snow draws his proof from another comparison
contenu_vulgarise:
The story goes that John Snow stopped the Soho cholera epidemic by having the handle of a Broad Street pump removed on September 8, 1854. Snow's own figures say otherwise.

## An Epidemic Already Receding

In *On the Mode of Communication of Cholera* (1855), Snow reconstructs the day of onset of the cases. The epidemic breaks out in the night of August 31 to September 1, and the largest number of attacks in a single day falls on September 1. The next day, they go from 143 to 116, then to 54. On September 8, the day the handle is removed, there are 12. They fall to 11 on the 9th, to 5 on the 10th and 11th, to 1 on the 12th.

Snow himself draws the consequence. In the letter he publishes in the *Medical Times and Gazette* on September 23, 1854, he writes that the number of attacks had decreased before the measure. In 1855, he adds that mortality had been greatly reduced by the flight of the population, and that it is impossible to decide whether the well still contained the cholera poison. A team of historians and epidemiologists (Brody and colleagues, *The Lancet*, 2000) holds the account of a removal that supposedly ended the epidemic to be apocryphal.

## Where the Proof Lies

Snow does not rely on this removal. His strongest demonstration concerns south London, and it fits in a table. Two water companies supply the city there: the Southwark and Vauxhall distributes water that contains London's sewage, Lambeth, water that is free of it. In one part of the south of the capital, their pipes intermingle in the most intimate way: the pipes of both companies run along every street, and each house depends on one or the other according to a choice made years earlier, when the companies were competing.

For the first seven weeks of the 1854 epidemic, Snow divides cholera deaths by the number of houses each company serves, according to a return made to Parliament for 1853. Southwark and Vauxhall: 1,263 deaths for 40,046 houses, or 315 per 10,000 houses. Lambeth: 98 deaths for 26,107 houses, or 37 per 10,000. These totals cover all the houses of each company, including in districts supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall alone.

It is the mixing of the pipes in the shared area that makes the two groups comparable. Snow writes that, in these districts, there is no difference between the houses or the inhabitants served by the two companies, and that no experiment could have tested the effect of water more completely. He speaks of an experiment carried out on the largest scale: at least three hundred thousand people, of all ages and ranks, find themselves divided into two groups without having chosen it, and most often without knowing it.

## The Shift

The pump is a scene: one man, one gesture, one street. The table has nothing spectacular about it, and yet it is what isolates a cause, because the two groups resemble each other in everything else. Snow himself does not settle, in 1855, the question of whether the Broad Street well was still contaminated on the day the handle was removed.

repere.texte: In Snow's Table IX, houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall company recorded 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses during the first seven weeks of 1854, against 37 for those of the Lambeth company.
repere.source: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed., London, John Churchill, 1855, Table IX

carte.punch: The Broad Street handle was removed when the epidemic was already receding.
carte.idee: On September 8, 1854, Snow counts 12 cholera attacks, against 143 on the 1st. His real proof is a table: 315 deaths per 10,000 houses for one water company, 37 for the other. The mixing of their pipes in one part of south London makes the two groups comparable.

quiz.question: Why does the removal of the handle not prove that the pump caused the epidemic?
choix: Attacks had already been falling since September 1, and part of the population had fled
Snow then believed in airborne transmission and the pump changed his mind
The handle was removed only in December, when the epidemic was over
Snow in fact never obtained the removal of the handle
quiz.explication: According to Snow, attacks go from 143 on September 1 to 12 on the 8th, the day of the removal, and the flight of the population also reduced mortality. The handle is not removed in December but on September 8, following his meeting with the parish, and Snow suspected the water before 1854.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why are the residents of the two water companies comparable, according to Snow, where their pipes intermingle?
choix: They were in two districts chosen for their similarity
The residents had been drawn by lot by the companies
Their pipes served the same streets, for rich and poor alike
They consumed the same quantity of water per inhabitant
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Snow insists on the mixing of the pipes: in one part of south London, each company serves houses on the same streets, large and small, according to a choice made when they were competing. It is neither a random draw nor two matched districts, and he does not measure consumption per person.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the daily attacks counted by Snow, from 143 on September 1 to 12 on the 8th, show?
choix: That the removal of the handle made cases drop overnight
That the epidemic was clearly receding before the handle was removed
That the epidemic reached its peak on the day of the removal
That cases resumed as soon as the handle was removed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Snow counts 143 attacks on September 1, 116 on the 2nd, 54 on the 3rd, and 12 on the 8th, the day of the removal. The decline predates the measure: the peak is not on the 8th, cases do not resume, and he still counts 11 on the 9th.
